The company behind a filing: who, how big, audited how, and doing what

Source: R/xbrl_company.R
xbrl_company.Rd

The background a set of accounts needs to be usable as statistics – identity, period, accounting class, auditor, employees, and the management's own description of what the company does and how the year went. One row per filing, ready to sit beside xbrl_lines() and xbrl_movements().

Usage

xbrl_company(x, persons = FALSE, prose = TRUE)

Arguments

x

A tibble from read_xbrl(). Every field here is read as text, so this is the one table that still works on a filing whose taxonomy version the package does not know.

persons

Include the names of the auditor, the executive and supervisory boards and the chairman of the general meeting. Off by default; see the section above.

prose

Include the free-text fields – the activity description, the year's development, events after the reporting period and the expected development. They can run to thousands of characters. FALSE keeps the row narrow for a table of many companies.

Value

A tibble with one row per filing, every field the filing carries about itself. A field it does not state is NA.

  • Identity: cvr, name, form, founded, period_start, period_end.

  • Where: street, postcode, city, country, registered_office.

  • Size and class: reporting_class, class, class_c_elements, employees, assets_not_owned, currency.

  • The report: report_type, general_meeting, approved, signature_place, submitter, submitter_cvr, xbrl_tool, policies_unchanged.

  • The audit: auditor_assistance, audit_firm, audit_firm_cvr, opinion, auditor_signed, audit_exempt.

  • With prose: activity, activity_source, development, development_source, events_after, expected_development, mortgages, contingent_liabilities.

  • With persons: auditor_name, auditor_id, auditor_description, executive_board, supervisory_board, chairman.

file comes last: the path the row was read from. xbrl_accounts() divides these into company, location, audit and prose.

What a filing reliably carries

Measured over 4,304 Danish and Greenlandic filings. Present in every one: the CVR number, the company's name, the accounting class, the type of auditor's assistance and the reporting period; the date of the general meeting is there in all but two. Then, in falling order: the executive board's names (94%), the address (82%), what the company does (79%), the audit firm and its CVR number (78%), how the year went (76%), the average number of employees (74%), when the company was founded (47%) and its registered office (45%). 99% say something about either their activity or their year.

The two prose figures are what this function returns, not what any single element carries – both fall back to a second element, and the _source columns say which answered.

The industry is not in the filing

The taxonomy has a place for it – IndustrySectorForEconomicActivitiesOfEntity – and not one filing of 4,304 uses it. Nor does any use SizeOfReportingEntityBySector. A company's industry has to come from the register instead, where it arrives as a code and a label in one field. No column is returned for it here, because a column that is empty in every row is worse than an absent one: it invites the reader to conclude the industry is unknown rather than that it was never asked for.

The legal form is not in the filing either, but the name has it

The taxonomy has no element for the reporting entity's own legal form. RelatedEntityLegalForm exists and is about the companies a filer is related to; there is nothing that says whether this one is an A/S or an ApS.

The name almost always does, because company law requires the form to be part of it. Measured over 4,304 filings, 99.6% carry a recognisable one: 3,330 ApS, 786 A/S, 120 IVS, 41 foundations and a handful of K/S and P/S. form is that reading.

The 17 that miss are mostly foundations named without "Fonden", and companies whose form is a compound – "Ejendomsaktieselskabet Illuut" – which is why the spelled-out Danish words are matched inside a word and the abbreviations are not: "ApS" as a syllable is a coincidence, "anpartsselskab" is not.

It is a reading of the name, not a reported fact, and it is here because the alternative is every caller writing the same regular expression. Where it matters, the register is the authority.

The activity description, and where it actually sits

The obvious element – DisclosureOfMainActivitiesAndAccountingAndFinancialMatters – is used by 6% of filings. The one companies actually use is DescriptionOfPrimaryActivitiesOfEntity, "virksomhedens væsentligste aktiviteter", at 72%. Both are read, the first as a fallback for the second.

development works the same way: the tagged description of the year at 54%, falling back to the management's review as a whole for a further 22% – which is a longer and looser text, so development_source says which was taken.

Two things the corpus taught this function

A headcount tagged to the nearest thousand. Six facts in 4,304 filings carry decimals = "-3" on the number of employees, and all six are the two filings that state 151,000 or 2,286,000 employees. No plausible fact carries it; the separation is exact. The filer's tool applied the statement's thousands-scaling to a headcount, and the same company states 2,296 in another year. Such a count is divided by a thousand. It moved the corpus mean from 780 employees to 19.8, and the maximum to Royal Greenland's real 2,296.

The accounting class is written in the filing's own language. 13 filings say "Reporting class B" where 4,112 say "Regnskabsklasse B", which splits a grouping in two without anyone noticing. reporting_class keeps the filing's own words – it is where "mikrovirksomhed" is visible – and class carries just the letter, which is the same in both languages.

Persons

A filing names people: the auditor, the executive board, the chairman of the general meeting. Those are personal data, and an accounts statistic does not need them – the audit firm and its CVR number answer "who audited this" without naming anyone. So they are left out unless asked for. Set persons = TRUE where there is a reason, and keep in mind that the result then carries names that should not be redistributed casually.

See also

xbrl_accounts(), which returns this beside the statements, and xbrl_lines() for the figures.

Other taxonomy: add_taxonomy(), check_breakdown(), check_cascade(), check_continuity(), check_inclusion(), check_movement(), check_statement(), read_taxonomy(), xbrl_accounts(), xbrl_fill(), xbrl_lines(), xbrl_movements(), xbrl_note_tables(), xbrl_period(), xbrl_resolve()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")
xbrl_company(x)

# with the names of the people who signed
xbrl_company(x, persons = TRUE)
} # }
